01

Introduction to Python Programming

Python is a high-level, interpreted, general-purpose programming language created by Guido van Rossum in 1991. Known for its simple, English-like syntax.

Key Features

  • Easy to read and write
  • Interpreted (runs line by line)
  • Dynamically typed
  • Platform independent

Used In

  • AI & Machine Learning
  • Web Development
  • Data Science
  • Automation / Scripting
print("Hello, World!")  # Your first Python program
02

Understanding Language — Human vs Computer

Computers only understand Machine Language (binary: 0s and 1s). Human-readable languages must be translated before the CPU can execute them.

LevelExampleUnderstood By
High-level languagex = 5 + 3Humans / Programmers
Assembly languageMOV AX, 5Low-level programmers
Machine language01001000 00000101CPU only
Python is a high-level language — very close to English, far from machine code. A translator (interpreter/compiler) bridges the gap.
03

Compilers and Interpreters

Compiler

Translates the entire source code into machine code at once before running.

  • Faster execution after compile
  • All errors shown at once
  • Creates a separate output file
  • Examples: C, C++

Interpreter

Translates and executes code line by line at runtime.

  • Easier to debug (error stops at that line)
  • Slower than compiled
  • No separate output file
  • Examples: Python, JavaScript
CompilerInterpreter
Translates whole program at onceTranslates line by line
Faster after compilationSlower execution
Generates object/exe fileNo file generated
Errors shown after full scanStops at first error
04

Hybrid Programming Languages

A hybrid language uses both a compiler and an interpreter. Source code is first compiled into an intermediate form called bytecode, which is then interpreted by a virtual machine.

# Python execution flow:
Source Code (.py)
    → Compiler  → Bytecode (.pyc)
    → PVM (Python Virtual Machine)
    → Output

Python (Hybrid)

Compiles .py → .pyc bytecode, then PVM interprets it.

Java (Hybrid)

Compiles .java → .class bytecode, then JVM interprets it.

This hybrid approach gives Python portability — the same bytecode runs on any machine that has the PVM installed.
05

Understanding Computer Programs

A computer program is a set of instructions that tells the computer how to solve a problem or perform a task.

Input

Data received from user, file, or network.

Processing

Calculations and logic applied to input.

Output

Result displayed to user or saved.

Storage

Data stored in variables, files, or databases.

name = input("Enter your name: ")   # Input
greeting = "Hello, " + name          # Processing
print(greeting)                       # Output
06

Understanding Variables in Python

A variable is a named memory location used to store a value. In Python, you don't declare a type — it is assigned automatically when a value is given.

age   = 20          # int — Python detects type automatically
name  = "Riya"      # str
marks = 98.5        # float
flag  = True        # bool

print(type(age))   # <class 'int'>
Think of a variable as a labelled box — the label is the name, the contents are the value. The contents can change anytime.
VariableValueType
age20int
name"Riya"str
marks98.5float
flagTruebool
07

Rules for Declaring Variables

  • Must start with a letter or underscore (_)
  • Cannot start with a number
  • Can contain letters, digits, and underscores only
  • Case-sensitive — Name and name are different variables
  • Cannot use Python reserved keywords (e.g. if, for, while, True…)
  • No spaces allowed in variable names
✓ Valid
my_var
_score
student1
totalMarks
✗ Invalid
2var  ← starts with number
my-var  ← hyphen not allowed
my var  ← space not allowed
for  ← reserved keyword
Convention: Use snake_case in Python — e.g. student_age, total_marks. Always use meaningful names.

Python Data Types (PyDT)

Every value in Python has a data type. Python detects the type automatically — this is called dynamic typing.

CategoryType(s)Example
Numericint, float, complex5, 3.14, 2+3j
Textstr"Hello"
BooleanboolTrue, False
Sequencelist, tuple, range[1, 2, 3]
Mappingdict{"key": "value"}

NoneNoneTypeNone
x = 10

09

Numeric Data Types — int & float

int (Integer)

Whole numbers — positive, negative, or zero. No decimal point. Unlimited size in Python 3.

float

Numbers with a decimal point or in scientific notation (e.g. 1.2e3 = 1200.0).

complex

Numbers with real + imaginary parts. Written as a + bj. Access parts via .real and .imag.

Arithmetic operators

+ add   - sub   * mul
/ div   // floor   % mod   ** power

a = 10       # int
b = 3.5      # float
c = 2+3j     # complex

print(a + b)    # 13.5   (int + float = float)
print(a // 3)  # 3      (floor division)
print(a % 3)   # 1      (remainder)
print(2 ** 4)  # 16     (2 to the power 4)
10

Literals & Constants

Literal — a fixed value written directly in code. It does not change.

TypeExample
Integer10, -3, 0
Float3.14, 0.5
String"Hi", 'World'
BooleanTrue, False
NoneNone

Constant — a variable whose value should never change. Python has no built-in constant keyword; use ALL_CAPS by convention.

PI      = 3.14159
GRAVITY = 9.8
MAX     = 100
ALL_CAPS is just a naming convention. Python won't prevent you from changing it — but you shouldn't!
11

Type Conversion

Implicit (Automatic)

Python automatically converts a smaller type to a larger one to avoid data loss.

x = 5      # int
y = 2.5    # float
z = x + y  # int → float
# z = 7.5, type: float

Explicit (Manual / Casting)

You force the conversion using built-in functions.

int("5")       # → 5
float(5)      # → 5.0
str(100)      # → "100"
bool(0)       # → False
bool(1)       # → True
FunctionConverts toExampleResult
int()Integerint("42")42
float()Floatfloat(5)5.0
str()Stringstr(99)"99"
bool()Booleanbool(0)False
complex()Complexcomplex(3)3+0j
int("3.5") → Error! Convert via float first: int(float("3.5")) → 3
